582.title: Hanuman carries them up
582.hook: the disguise comes off, and Hanuman carries two princes up the mountain
582.howItsDone: Images of Hanuman carrying Rama and Lakshmana on his shoulders are common in Hindu art. In many temples Hanuman's image stands near Rama's with hands joined, and many families recite the Hanuman Chalisa, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vakya, Hanuman's first words, and Rama's praise for them: true, kind, helpful speech is a practice. True, kind, helpful speech is a practice.
screen: `TRUE, KIND, HELPFUL SPEECH IS A PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Now it's Lakshmana's turn to answer, and he does something you might not expect from a wary prince in a dangerous forest. He tells the stranger everything. Who they are. Why they're in exile. That Sita has been taken by a rakshasa while they were away, and they don't know where. That Kabandha sent them to find Sugriva. A wary prince might give a stranger the short version. Lakshmana gives the whole thing.
screen: `LAKSHMANA ANSWERS.` → `HE TELLS IT ALL.` → `NOT THE SHORT VERSION.`

segments.voice: Trust answered with trust. Hanuman spoke carefully and honestly, and Lakshmana meets that with the whole story, including a humbling sentence for a prince of Ayodhya: Rama, who used to be a refuge for others, has come to Sugriva for refuge. Hanuman is glad. Sugriva too has lost his wife and his kingdom, he says. You can help each other. Then the disguise comes off. He takes his own shape, a monkey, the son of the Wind. Rishyamuka is steep and the brothers have walked a long way, so he lifts them onto his shoulders and carries them up the mountain to Sugriva. Here's why that picture matters so much to Hindus. Hanuman is the great example of dasya, devotion as service: loving God by doing God's work, with no wish to be the hero. Hindu teachers count dasya among the classic ways of devotion, and Hanuman is the one they point to. So Hindus don't pray to Hanuman instead of Rama. They pray to him on the way to Rama. In many temples his image stands near Rama's, hands joined. Many families recite the Hanuman Chalisa, forty verses traditionally credited to the poet Tulsidas, often on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and one line calls him the guardian at Rama's door. Today's scene is that line in action: the servant who carries tired people to Rama. As for his name, the old bear Jambavan tells that story much later. As a baby he leapt at the rising sun, thinking it was a fruit, and Indra's thunderbolt struck his jaw, his hanu.
screen: `TRUST ANSWERED WITH TRUST.` · `CARRIED UP THE MOUNTAIN.` · then, large: `DASYA: LOVE THAT SERVES.` · `HANU: THE STRUCK JAW.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop, and feel how much they carry on an ordinary day. If you pray, say the chant many Hindu families use, Shri Ram, jai Ram, jai jai Ram, softly on each out-breath, the way Hanuman keeps Rama's name. If you don't pray, breathe out slowly and bring to mind one person whose load you could help carry this week, without needing to be thanked.
Hanu, the jaw struck by Indra's thunderbolt, which gave Hanuman his name.
Your line: dasya, love that serves. Hanuman carries tired people to Rama and never asks to be the hero. Until tomorrow.

583.title: friends before the fire
583.hook: two exiles walk around a fire and become friends
583.carry: sakhya, friendship sworn before the fire
583.howItsDone: In a Hindu wedding the couple walks around the sacred fire with Agni called on as witness (the number of rounds and steps varies by custom); Rama and Sugriva's circling of the fire uses that same gesture for friendship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the disguise came off, Hanuman carried the brothers up the mountain, and we met dasya, love that serves.

Two exiles meet on a mountaintop. One is a prince who lost his kingdom and then his wife. The other is a monkey prince who lost his kingdom and his wife to his own brother. They've never seen each other before today. Both have been betrayed, or think they have. How do you start a friendship between two people with every reason to be careful? Valmiki's answer involves fire, and it's Hanuman who sets it up.
screen: `TWO EXILES MEET.` → `MATCHING LOSSES.` → `AN ANSWER WITH FIRE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman arranges it. He brings wood, kindles a fire between them, and honors it with flowers. Rama and Sugriva walk around the fire together, keeping it to their right, the way a bride and groom do at a Hindu wedding. Then they say to each other, in effect: from now on, your joy is my joy, and your sorrow is my sorrow. Why fire? In Hindu ritual, Agni, the fire, carries offerings to the gods and witnesses vows. That's the reason the fire sits at the center of a Hindu wedding: the couple's promises are made in front of a witness that can't be argued with. Rama and Sugriva use the same witness for a friendship. Then they make it equal. Sugriva breaks off a flowering branch and spreads it on the ground, and he and Rama sit on it together. Hanuman breaks off another for Lakshmana. Two exiles side by side: neither patron nor beggar. Then, what each one needs. Sugriva's brother Vali has taken his kingdom and his wife. Rama promises to deal with Vali. Sugriva promises to help find Sita. It's a deal, yes, but the poem frames it as friendship first. The word is sakhya, the bond of a sakha, a friend. Later the Bhagavata Purana counts sakhya among the ways of loving God: God as a friend, the way Arjuna loves Krishna. So in this tradition, friendship isn't small. Sworn honestly, it can be holy.
screen: `AROUND THE FIRE, TOGETHER.` · `AGNI AS WITNESS.` · `TWO EXILES ON ONE BRANCH.` · then, large: `SAKHYA: FRIENDSHIP, SWORN.`

segments.voice: If you have a diya or a candle, light it; if not, picture a small flame in front of you. Bring one friend to mind. Breathe in and remember a time their sorrow felt like yours; breathe out and remember a time their joy did too. If you pray, hold them before the flame, the way Rama and Sugriva held their promise before Agni.
Sakhya, the bond of a sakha, a friend: sworn today around a fire between Rama and Sugriva, your joy is mine and your sorrow is mine.
Your line: sakhya, friendship sworn before the fire. Your joy is my joy, your sorrow is my sorrow. Day five hundred eighty-three, done.

584.title: I know only the anklets
584.hook: a bundle of jewels, and a brother-in-law who only knows the anklets
584.carry: touching an elder's feet is honor
584.howItsDone: Touching the feet of parents, teachers and elders (pranam or charan sparsh) is a common gesture of respect in many Hindu families, and Lakshmana's words about the anklets are often quoted when it's explained.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama and Sugriva circled the fire. Sakhya, friendship sworn before the fire, with Agni as witness.

Sugriva has something to show Rama. A while ago, he says, five of us were sitting up here, and we saw a rakshasa flying across the sky carrying a woman. She was crying out: Rama, Lakshmana. When she saw us below, she dropped her upper cloth and some of her jewelry, tied in a bundle. We kept them safe. He sends someone into the cave to bring them out.
screen: `FIVE OF US, ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `A WOMAN CRYING OUT.` → `A BUNDLE DROPPED.`

segments.voice: Rama sees the cloth and the ornaments and breaks down. He presses them to his chest and weeps. Sita did more than call out. She left a trail, throwing down what she could to five strangers, hoping someone would get it to Rama. Someone did. Then Rama turns to Lakshmana: do you know these? Lakshmana's answer isn't what you'd expect. I don't know her armlets, he says. I don't know her earrings. But I know the anklets, because I bowed at her feet every day. Through all the years in the forest, Lakshmana kept his eyes lowered before his brother's wife, the way you would before a mother. And that verse is quoted to explain a gesture you'll see in Hindu homes everywhere: bending to touch the feet of parents, grandparents and teachers, often called pranam or charan sparsh. The feet are the humblest part of a person. Touching them says: I put my pride below you, and I ask your blessing. Often the elder answers with a hand on your head. It isn't groveling; it's honor that goes low on purpose. Then the pact becomes real. Rama asks: who took her, and where? Sugriva admits he doesn't know where Ravana lives, but he promises to find out, and that Rama will have Sita back. A friendship sworn before the fire now has something to hold in its hands.
screen: `SITA LEFT A TRAIL.` · `I KNOW ONLY THE ANKLETS.` · `EYES LOWERED, IN RESPECT.` · then, large: `TOUCHING AN ELDER'S FEET.`

segments.voice: Let your gaze drop softly to your own feet. Breathe in and think of someone you honor, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher; breathe out and offer them, silently, the bow Lakshmana gave every day. If that person is near you this week, you might bend and touch their feet, or simply join your hands. Keep your eyes low and your breath slow.

585.title: Rama's word
585.hook: a feud built on a sealed cave, and a promise that has to prove itself
585.carry: a promise given once is kept
585.howItsDone: The seven sala trees and Dundubhi's bones are favorite scenes in Ramayana art and storytelling, and sites near Hampi in Karnataka are traditionally linked to Kishkindha, Rishyamuka and Vali's cave.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's jewels came out, Lakshmana knew only the anklets, and we saw why touching an elder's feet is honor.

Rama has promised to kill Vali. Sugriva has a question he's too polite to ask out loud: can you? Vali is famous. He's so strong he used to stride between the eastern and western seas before sunrise. Sugriva has watched that strength up close, and he has run from it. A friend with a bow is good news, but he needs to know this friend is enough. So Sugriva tells a story. And then he points at some trees.
screen: `A QUESTION TOO POLITE TO ASK.` → `A STORY, THEN SOME TREES.`

segments.voice: First, the story of the brothers. Vali, the elder, ruled Kishkindha, and Sugriva served him. One night a demon named Mayavi came to the gate shouting a challenge. Vali chased him into a huge cave and told Sugriva to wait at the mouth. A long time passed. Then blood came foaming out, and Sugriva heard the demon roar but not his brother. Sure Vali was dead, he sealed the cave with a boulder and went home, and the ministers made him king. But Vali had won. He came out, found the cave blocked and his brother on his throne, believed he'd been betrayed, and drove Sugriva out. Then the test. Sugriva shows Rama the dried skeleton of a buffalo demon Vali once killed, and Rama flicks it far away with his toe. It's dry now, Sugriva says politely. So he points to seven huge sala trees. Rama fires once. The arrow goes through all seven, through the hill behind them, into the earth, and back to his quiver. Sugriva falls at his feet. Notice what he was really asking. He never doubted Rama's heart; he needed to know the promise could be kept. And keeping a promise is what the tradition loves most about Rama. Back in Ayodhya, Valmiki has Rama tell Kaikeyi: Rama does not speak twice. His word, once given, stands. Centuries later the poet Tulsidas put it in a line many Hindi-speaking families know by heart: in Raghu's family, life may go, but a given word, a vachan, may not. Keeping it is satya, truth, a mark of dharma. Rama isn't offended by the test. He simply shows that his word and his power line up.
screen: `MAYAVI AND THE SEALED CAVE.` · `VALI RETURNS. A DEMON'S SKELETON.` · `ONE ARROW, SEVEN SALA TREES.` · then, large: `RAMA DOES NOT SPEAK TWICE.`

If you pray, offer that promise before God, the way Rama and Sugriva made theirs before the fire. Let your shoulders loosen; a kept word is lighter to carry.

586.title: Vali's question
586.hook: an arrow from cover, and a question the tradition still discusses
586.carry: dharma is subtle, and may be questioned
586.howItsDone: Vali's death is discussed at length in Ramayana commentary; traditional commentators defend Rama's action in several ways, while some later tellings and modern readers question it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: one arrow through seven sala trees, and Rama's word. A promise given once is kept.

Two brothers fight at a city gate. A third man, hidden behind trees with a bow, shoots one of them. And the dying brother asks a question that tellers, poets and commentators have answered in different ways. The Ramayana doesn't make this scene easy. So today, just hear it as Valmiki tells it: who does what, who says what, and in what order. Where you land afterward is up to you; the tradition has room for more than one view.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS AT THE GATE.` → `AN ARROW FROM COVER.` → `THE DYING BROTHER'S QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Sugriva goes to Kishkindha's gate and roars a challenge. Vali comes out, and the brothers fight. Rama, watching from cover, doesn't shoot: the brothers look so alike he can't tell them apart. Sugriva is beaten and flees. So Lakshmana hangs a flowering creeper around his neck, so Rama will know him. Second challenge. This time Vali's wife Tara stops him at the door. Sugriva lost to you only today and he's back roaring, she says. He must have a powerful ally. I've heard it's Rama. Don't go. Vali goes anyway: Rama is righteous, he says, he won't do wrong. The fight begins, Vali starts to win, and Rama shoots. Dying, Vali speaks, and it's an accusation. I wasn't fighting you. You struck from hiding while I fought someone else. What wrong had I done you? Rama answers at length. This land is under the rule of Bharata's line, and I act for that rule. You took your brother's wife while he lived. And kings hunt from cover. And he says something Hindus have leaned on ever since: dharma is subtle, and hard to know. Dharma isn't a referee's rulebook. It's right action weighed in a real situation, and good people can weigh it differently. In the text, Vali accepts the answer. Some readers find it enough; others, including commentators and poets, find the scene troubling, and some later tellings change it. Valmiki keeps both the question and the answer. That's the teaching: in this tradition, even Rama's choices can be honestly questioned.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS TOO ALIKE TO TELL.` · `TARA'S WARNING.` · `VALI'S QUESTION, RAMA'S ANSWER.` · then, large: `DHARMA IS SUBTLE.`

segments.voice: Sit with a question that doesn't resolve easily, from today's story or from your own life. Breathe in and let it be there; breathe out and don't answer it yet. If you pray, offer the question itself, not a verdict. Each time you start arguing with yourself, come back to the breath.

587.title: Tara's lament
587.hook: a widow runs toward the battlefield, and a son lights his father's pyre
587.carry: antyeshti, the last rite, and room to grieve
587.howItsDone: Most Hindus cremate their dead; a son traditionally lights the pyre, though daughters and other relatives now often do, and a mourning period of around ten to thirteen days follows, by family custom. Tara is also honored as one of the panchakanya, five women named in a verse some recite in the morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vali's question and Rama's answer. Dharma is subtle, and may be questioned.

Word reaches the palace: Vali is down. The monkeys who saw it want to run, or hide, or shut the gates against Rama. Tara doesn't. She was the one who warned him, earlier that same day, and he didn't listen. Now she runs the other way, out of the city, past the frightened crowd, toward the place where her husband is lying with an arrow in his chest. Her son Angada is with her.
screen: `VALI IS DOWN.` → `THE CROWD RUNS AWAY.` → `TARA RUNS TOWARD HIM.`

segments.voice: Tara reaches Vali and falls beside him, and Valmiki gives her lament in full. She speaks to Vali: you lie on the bare earth as if you loved it more than me. She speaks bitterly to Sugriva: now you have the kingdom. She even begs Rama to let her follow her husband. In the middle of an adventure story, the poem stops for a widow's grief and lets it be angry. Then Vali's last words. He speaks to Sugriva without anger now: fate caught us both, more or less. He asks him to raise Angada as his own son and to listen to Tara, who sees things before anyone else. He puts Indra's golden necklace on his brother, and dies. Sugriva breaks. Now that he's won, he'd rather have his brother than the throne. Rama, who fired the arrow, steadies them all and tells them to perform the rites. And Angada lights his father's pyre. This is antyeshti, the last rite, the final one of the samskaras that mark a Hindu life from birth to death. Most Hindus cremate. Agni, the same fire that witnesses a wedding, receives the body and returns it to the elements, while the atman, the self, is understood not to die. Traditionally a son lights the fire; today daughters and others often do too. Then come days set aside for mourning, often ten to thirteen, depending on the family. Notice Valmiki's order: the grief first, full and untidy, then the rite. The tradition doesn't ask mourners to be neat.
screen: `TARA'S LAMENT, IN FULL.` · `VALI'S LAST WORDS.` · `ANGADA LIGHTS THE PYRE.` · then, large: `ANTYESHTI, AND ROOM TO GRIEVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a loss, large or small, yours or someone else's, without pushing it away. Breathe in and let the feeling be its real size; breathe out and let your body hold it. If you pray, many Hindus remember the dead with a lamp and a quiet om shanti. And if grief ever turns into thoughts of hurting yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

588.title: four months of rain
588.hook: a new king goes to his palace, and the man who made him king goes to a cave
588.carry: chaturmas, the four holy months of rain
588.howItsDone: The four months of the rainy season, chaturmasa, are still kept by some Hindu ascetics and households as a time to stay in one place, travel less, and take on extra vows and study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tara's lament, Vali's last words, and Angada at the pyre. Antyeshti, the last rite, and room to grieve. Today the week closes.

Sugriva is crowned. Angada is named heir. The city celebrates with drums and garlands. And Rama doesn't go in. He's an exile, he says, and he promised fourteen years outside any village or town. So the new king of Kishkindha goes to his palace, and the man who made him king walks off to live in a cave. Valmiki doesn't rush past it: the city lit up, and two brothers walking away from it into the hills.
screen: `SUGRIVA CROWNED.` → `RAMA WON'T GO IN.` → `TWO BROTHERS WALK TO THE HILLS.`

segments.voice: It's the start of the rainy season. Rama explains: you can't send search parties across the land in the monsoon. Rivers flood, roads vanish. Enjoy your kingdom for these months, he tells Sugriva; when autumn comes, we search. So Rama and Lakshmana go to a mountain called Prasravana and find a wide cave to wait out the rain. Four months, and nothing to do but wait, for a man whose wife is a prisoner somewhere he can't even name. Lakshmana makes it bearable. When Rama sinks into grief, Lakshmana reminds him who he is, and to save his strength for the time to act. And Valmiki fills the chapter with what they see: peaks, rushing water, flowering trees, birds. Hindus still keep these months. They're called chaturmas, the four months. Many traditions say Vishnu goes into his deep sleep on Devshayani Ekadashi, early in the rains, and wakes on Prabodhini Ekadashi in the autumn month of Kartik. Through that season many monks stop wandering and stay in one place, and many households take on a vow: giving up a food, reading a scripture, adding a prayer. Some teachers read Rama's cave as that season in story form: when you can't move, you keep your vow and gather strength. Now the week, by its teachings: dasya, love that serves. Sakhya, friendship sworn before the fire. Touching an elder's feet. A promise given once is kept. Dharma is subtle. Antyeshti, the last rite. And today, chaturmas, and the rain coming in.
screen: `NO SEARCHING IN THE MONSOON.` · `THE CAVE ON PRASRAVANA.` · `CHATURMAS: THE FOUR MONTHS.` · `KEEP A VOW, GATHER STRENGTH.` · then, large: `THE WEEK, AND THE RAIN COMING IN.`

segments.voice: Listen. If there's rain, listen to it; if not, to whatever's there: traffic, a fan, your own breath. Let the sound be the whole practice. If you pray, choose one small vow for this season, the way families do for chaturmas: one food, one page, one prayer. If you don't, choose one small steady habit to keep while you wait for something.
